submodules.title: 1. What Are Derivatives?
submodules.intro: What is a contract whose value comes from something else?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: WHAT ARE DERIVATIVES?
A derivative is a contract whose value is derived from something else, called the underlying. The underlying can be a share, an index like the Nifty 50, a currency or a commodity. People use derivatives to protect against price changes, which is called hedging, or to bet on price changes, which is called speculation. Derivatives are high-risk and only for adults, so use this lesson to learn and practise on a simulator. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
The story goes that the Greek philosopher Thales once paid a small fee to reserve olive presses before a big harvest, which worked a bit like an option. Ideas like this are thousands of years old.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE KEY IDEAS
• Underlying: the thing the contract follows, such as a share or an index.
• Contract: an agreement about a future price, date and quantity.
• Hedging: using a derivative to reduce a risk you already have.
• Speculation: using a derivative to bet on a price move, which adds risk.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: FORWARDS AND FUTURES
• A forward is a private deal between two parties to trade at a fixed price on a future date.
• A futures contract is the same idea, but standardised and traded on an exchange, with a clearing corporation standing between buyer and seller to reduce the risk of someone not paying.
• Options are another kind of derivative, covered in later lessons.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHY THEY MATTER
• Businesses use derivatives to fix costs, such as a bakery fixing its wheat price.
• Investors use them to protect a portfolio.
• The same tools used carelessly can cause big losses very quickly.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE BAKERY'S WHEAT
A fictional bakery agrees today to buy 100 kg of wheat in 3 months at ₹30 per kg, a total of ₹3,000. If the market price rises to ₹36, the bakery saves (36 - 30) x 100 = ₹600. If the price falls to ₹26, it pays (30 - 26) x 100 = ₹400 more than the market. Aarav says the deal was a loss in the second case. Meera says the bakery wanted certainty about its cost, and it got it.

🧪 TRY IT: LOCK THE PRICE
A fictional rice trader agrees to sell 50 kg of rice in 3 months at ₹40 per kg. If the market price turns out to be ₹34, who gains and by how much? What if it turns out to be ₹45?
(Answer: at ₹34, the trader gains (40 - 34) x 50 = ₹300 compared with the market. At ₹45, the trader gives up (45 - 40) x 50 = ₹250. The locked price gave certainty, not a guaranteed win.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
A derivative is a contract that follows an underlying. It can reduce risk when used for hedging and add risk when used for speculation.

quiz.question: What is a derivative?

quiz.explanation: A derivative's value is derived from something else, the underlying.

options: A share, an index, a currency or a commodity
quiz.explanation: Underlyings include shares, indices, currencies and commodities.

quiz.question: A bakery locks wheat at ₹30 per kg for 100 kg. The market price becomes ₹36. How much does it save?
What is hedging?
options: Using a derivative to reduce an existing risk
quiz.explanation: Hedging aims to lower a risk you already have.

quiz.question: How is a futures contract different from a forward?
options: It is standardised and traded on an exchange
quiz.explanation: Futures are standardised exchange contracts, while forwards are private deals.

submodules.title: 2. Futures Basics
submodules.intro: What happens when you agree today to trade at a set price later?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: FUTURES BASICS
A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell an underlying at a fixed price on a fixed date. Both sides are obliged to follow through, and profit or loss is settled every day. Because the exposure is large, futures can turn small price moves into big gains and big losses. Derivatives are high-risk and only for adults, so use this lesson to learn and practise on a simulator. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A futures buyer and seller are both committed. Unlike an option buyer, neither can simply walk away by losing a small fee.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE TERMS
• Lot size: futures trade in fixed bundles, such as 100 shares per lot. You cannot buy just one share.
• Expiry: the date the contract ends. The exchange sets these dates and they can change.
• Long: you buy and profit when the price rises.
• Short: you sell and profit when the price falls.
• Profit or loss = (price now - entry price) x lot size for a long. A short is the opposite.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: DAILY SETTLEMENT
• Mark-to-market means gains and losses are added to or taken from your account every day, not only at the end.
• If losses eat into your deposit, you must top it up or the position can be closed.
• Index futures are settled in cash. Stock futures in India are settled by delivery of shares.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHY PEOPLE USE THEM
• To hedge a portfolio quickly, such as shorting index futures against a share portfolio.
• To take a view on the whole market without picking one share.
• To speculate, which is the riskiest use.

🍕 MINI CASE: ONE LOT, TWO OUTCOMES
In her simulator, Meera buys one lot of a fictional share future at ₹200. The lot size is 100. If the price rises to ₹210, her profit is (210 - 200) x 100 = ₹1,000. If it falls to ₹195, her loss is (200 - 195) x 100 = ₹500. A trader who sold at ₹200 would have the exact opposite results. Aarav notes that one side's gain is always the other side's loss.

🧪 TRY IT: SHORT IT
In a simulator, a trader sells one lot of 50 shares of a fictional share future at ₹500. The price falls to ₹480. What is the profit or loss?
(Answer: a short profits when price falls. (500 - 480) x 50 = ₹1,000 profit. If the price had risen to ₹520, the loss would be ₹1,000.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Futures commit both sides to a price and a date, are settled every day, and move in lot-sized steps. Both gains and losses can be large.

quiz.question: What does a long futures position profit from?
quiz.explanation: A long position gains when the price rises.

quiz.question: You buy one lot of 100 at ₹200 and the price becomes ₹210. What is the profit?
What is a lot size?
options: The fixed bundle in which a contract trades
quiz.explanation: Futures trade in fixed lots, such as 100 shares.

quiz.question: What does mark-to-market mean?
options: Profit and loss are settled every day
quiz.explanation: Gains and losses are added or deducted daily.

quiz.question: A short position profits when...
quiz.explanation: A short sells first and profits if the price drops.

submodules.title: 3. Margin and Leverage
submodules.intro: How can a small deposit control a large position, and what is the catch?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: MARGIN AND LEVERAGE
To trade futures you do not pay the full value of the contract. You put up a smaller deposit called margin. This gives leverage, which magnifies results in both directions. Leverage is the main reason derivatives are so risky. Derivatives are high-risk and only for adults, so use this lesson to learn and practise on a simulator. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
With 5 times leverage, a 20% fall in the price can wipe out your entire margin.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE MATHS OF LEVERAGE
• Contract value = price x lot size.
• Margin = a percentage of the contract value, set by the exchange and broker.
• Leverage = contract value ÷ margin.
• Loss as a % of margin = % price move x leverage.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: MARGIN CALLS
• If losses use up part of the margin, you may have to add more money, called a margin call.
• If you do not, the broker can close your position at a loss.
• Losses can be larger than the margin you put up.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: USING LEVERAGE SAFELY
• Size the position by the loss you can accept, not by the margin available.
• Keep spare cash in the account so a small swing does not force you out.
• Remember that leverage also magnifies gains, which can tempt people to take too much.

🍕 MINI CASE: A 10% FALL, A 50% LOSS
A fictional futures contract is priced at ₹200 with a lot size of 100, so the contract value is ₹20,000. The margin is 20%, which is ₹4,000, so leverage is 20,000 ÷ 4,000 = 5 times. The price falls 10%, which is a loss of 20,000 x 0.10 = ₹2,000. That is 2,000 ÷ 4,000 = 50% of the margin. A 20% fall would lose ₹4,000, the whole margin.

🧪 TRY IT: WORK OUT THE HIT
A fictional contract has a price of ₹500 and a lot size of 50. The margin is 20%. What are the contract value and margin, and what share of the margin is lost if the price falls 8%?
(Answer: the contract value is 500 x 50 = ₹25,000 and the margin is ₹5,000. An 8% fall is a loss of 25,000 x 0.08 = ₹2,000, which is 2,000 ÷ 5,000 = 40% of the margin.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Margin lets a small deposit control a large position, which magnifies gains and losses. Size positions by the loss you can accept, not by the margin you have.

quiz.question: What is margin?
options: A deposit that is a part of the contract value
The full price of the contract
quiz.explanation: Margin is a smaller deposit, not the full value.

quiz.question: Contract value is ₹20,000 and margin is ₹4,000. What is the leverage?
With 5 times leverage, a 10% price fall loses what share of the margin?
quiz.explanation: 10% x 5 = 50% of the margin.

quiz.question: What is a margin call?
options: A demand to add money when losses reduce your margin
quiz.explanation: You must top up the account or the position may be closed.

quiz.question: Can derivative losses exceed the margin you put up?
quiz.explanation: Leverage means losses can be larger than the deposit.

submodules.title: 4. Futures Pricing: Cost of Carry and Basis
submodules.intro: Why does a future cost different from today's price?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: FUTURES PRICING AND BASIS
A futures price is usually not equal to today's price, which is called the spot price. The gap comes from the cost of holding the underlying until expiry. Understanding it explains why futures prices drift toward spot as expiry nears. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
On the day of expiry, the futures price and the spot price become the same, which is called convergence.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: COST OF CARRY
• Simple fair value = Spot x (1 + interest rate x time in years).
• The idea: instead of buying the share now, you hold your money and earn interest, so the future costs a little more.
• Expected dividends reduce the futures price, because the holder of the share would receive them.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: BASIS
• Basis = futures price - spot price.
• A positive basis is common and is called contango.
• Basis shrinks toward zero as expiry gets closer.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHAT IT MEANS FOR TRADERS
• A futures price is not a forecast that the share will rise.
• If you roll a futures position into the next month, you pay the new month's higher price, which is a cost.
• Large differences from fair value can attract arbitrage, where traders lock in tiny risk-free gaps, which keeps prices aligned.

🍕 MINI CASE: FAIR VALUE OF A FUTURE
A fictional share has a spot price of ₹100. The yearly interest rate is 6% and the contract expires in 3 months, which is 0.25 years. Fair value = 100 x (1 + 0.06 x 0.25) = 100 x 1.015 = ₹101.50. The basis is 101.50 - 100 = ₹1.50. Aarav says the market expects a rise. Meera says it only reflects the interest cost of waiting.

🧪 TRY IT: PRICE THE FUTURE
A fictional share has a spot price of ₹200. The yearly rate is 8% and the contract expires in 6 months. What is the simple fair value of the future, and what is the basis?
(Answer: 200 x (1 + 0.08 x 0.5) = 200 x 1.04 = ₹208. The basis is 208 - 200 = ₹8.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Futures price reflects the cost of carry, not a forecast. The basis shrinks as expiry nears, and the futures price meets the spot price at expiry.

quiz.question: What is the basis?
quiz.explanation: Basis = futures price - spot price.

quiz.question: Spot is ₹100, rate is 6% a year, expiry in 3 months. What is the simple fair value?
What happens to the basis as expiry gets close?
quiz.explanation: Futures and spot converge at expiry.

quiz.question: Does a futures price above spot mean the market expects a rise?
options: No, it mostly reflects the cost of carry
quiz.explanation: The gap mostly reflects interest cost, not a forecast.

quiz.question: How do expected dividends affect the futures price?
quiz.explanation: The share holder receives dividends, so the future is priced a bit lower.

submodules.title: 5. Options Basics: Calls and Puts
submodules.intro: What if you could buy the right, but not the duty, to trade later?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: OPTIONS BASICS
An option gives the buyer the right, but not the duty, to buy or sell an underlying at a set price on or before a set date. The buyer pays a price for this right, called the premium. This is very different from futures, where both sides are committed. Derivatives are high-risk and only for adults, so use this lesson to learn and practise on a simulator. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
An option buyer can never lose more than the premium paid, but an option seller can lose far more than the premium received.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE TERMS
• Call option: the right to buy at the strike price.
• Put option: the right to sell at the strike price.
• Strike price: the fixed price in the contract.
• Premium: the price of the option, paid by the buyer to the seller.
• Expiry: the last date. Index options are settled in cash.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: BUYER AND SELLER
• Buyer: pays the premium, has limited loss (the premium) and potentially large gain.
• Seller (writer): receives the premium, has limited gain (the premium) and potentially very large loss.
• The seller must put up margin because of that large risk.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: COST OF AN OPTION POSITION
• Total premium = premium per share x lot size.
• An option that is cheap can still lose its whole price quickly, so a cheap price is not a safe price.

🍕 MINI CASE: BUYING A CALL IN THE SIMULATOR
Meera buys one lot of a fictional call option in her simulator. The strike is ₹200, the premium is ₹8 and the lot size is 100. Her total cost is 8 x 100 = ₹800, which is also the most she can lose. If the share stays below ₹200 at expiry, the option expires worthless and she loses ₹800. The seller keeps the ₹800 but must buy or sell if the option is used.

🧪 TRY IT: COUNT THE PREMIUM
A fictional put option has a strike of ₹300, a premium of ₹10 and a lot size of 50. What does the buyer pay in total, and what is the most the buyer can lose?
(Answer: the total premium is 10 x 50 = ₹500, and that is also the most the buyer can lose.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Calls give the right to buy and puts give the right to sell. Buyers risk only the premium, while sellers take on large risk for a small premium.

quiz.question: What does a call option give the buyer?
options: The right to buy at the strike price
quiz.explanation: A call gives the right, not the duty, to buy.

quiz.question: What does a put option give the buyer?
options: The right to sell at the strike price
The right to buy for free
quiz.explanation: A put gives the right to sell at the strike.

quiz.question: A call has a premium of ₹8 and a lot size of 100. What is the total cost?
What is the most an option buyer can lose?
quiz.explanation: The buyer's loss is capped at the premium.

quiz.question: Why must option sellers be especially careful?
options: They can lose far more than the premium they received
quiz.explanation: The seller's gain is capped but the loss can be very large.

submodules.title: 6. Option Payoffs and Breakeven
submodules.intro: How far does the price have to move before an option buyer earns a profit?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: OPTION PAYOFFS AND BREAKEVEN
An option's result at expiry depends on where the underlying finishes compared with the strike, and on the premium paid. The premium is a cost the price must first overcome. Learning to draw the payoff in your head helps you see the risk before you act. Derivatives are high-risk and only for adults, so use this lesson to learn and practise on a simulator. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A call buyer can be right about the direction of a share and still lose money if the move is too small to cover the premium.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: LONG CALL AT EXPIRY
• Payoff per share = the larger of (price - strike) or 0.
• Profit per share = payoff - premium.
• Breakeven = strike + premium.
• Maximum loss = premium. Profit grows as the price rises.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: LONG PUT AT EXPIRY
• Payoff per share = the larger of (strike - price) or 0.
• Profit per share = payoff - premium.
• Breakeven = strike - premium.
• Maximum loss = premium. Profit grows as the price falls.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: READING IT RIGHT
• Multiply per-share results by the lot size to get rupees.
• Between the strike and the breakeven, the option has some value but you still lose money overall.
• These results apply at expiry. Before expiry, the option price also depends on time and volatility.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE CALL, AT THREE PRICES
Meera's fictional call has a strike of ₹200, a premium of ₹8 and a lot size of 100. Breakeven is 200 + 8 = ₹208. At ₹220, profit per share is (220 - 200) - 8 = ₹12, so ₹1,200 per lot. At ₹205, the payoff is 5 but the premium was 8, so the loss is ₹3 per share, ₹300 per lot. At ₹190, the option expires worthless and the loss is the full ₹800.

🧪 TRY IT: PUT PAYOFF
A fictional put has a strike of ₹300, a premium of ₹10 and a lot size of 50. At expiry the share is at ₹270. What is the breakeven, and what is the profit per lot?
(Answer: breakeven = 300 - 10 = ₹290. At ₹270, the payoff is 30 and profit per share is 30 - 10 = ₹20, so 20 x 50 = ₹1,000 per lot.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Calls need the price to rise above strike plus premium, and puts need it to fall below strike minus premium. The premium is a hurdle you must clear first.

quiz.question: A call has a strike of ₹200 and a premium of ₹8. What is the breakeven at expiry?
quiz.explanation: Breakeven = strike + premium = 208.

quiz.question: The same call expires with the share at ₹220. What is the profit per share?
The same call expires with the share at ₹190. What is the result?
quiz.explanation: It expires worthless, so the premium is lost.

quiz.question: A put has a strike of ₹300 and a premium of ₹10. What is the breakeven?
quiz.explanation: Breakeven = strike - premium = 290.

quiz.question: A call buyer is right about direction, but the move is smaller than the premium. What happens?
quiz.explanation: The price must clear the premium before there is a profit.

submodules.title: 7. Intrinsic Value, Time Value and Moneyness
submodules.intro: What are you really paying for when you buy an option?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: INTRINSIC VALUE, TIME VALUE AND MONEYNESS
An option's premium has two parts. Intrinsic value is the amount it is worth if used right now. Time value is the extra you pay for the chance that things move in your favour before expiry. Knowing the two parts shows why some options are so likely to lose money. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
At the moment of expiry, an option has no time value left. Its price is only its intrinsic value.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: INTRINSIC VALUE
• Call intrinsic value = the larger of (price - strike) or 0.
• Put intrinsic value = the larger of (strike - price) or 0.
• Premium = intrinsic value + time value.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: MONEYNESS
• In the money (ITM): the option has intrinsic value. A call is ITM when price is above strike.
• At the money (ATM): the strike is close to the current price.
• Out of the money (OTM): no intrinsic value. A call is OTM when price is below strike.
• An OTM option is all time value, so it is cheap, but it often expires worthless.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: A COMMON TRAP
• Far OTM options look cheap, so beginners buy many of them, then lose the premium again and again.
• The cheapness reflects a low chance of success, not a bargain.

🍕 MINI CASE: SPLITTING THE PREMIUM
A fictional share trades at ₹210. A call with a strike of ₹200 has a premium of ₹15. Its intrinsic value is 210 - 200 = ₹10, so its time value is 15 - 10 = ₹5. A call with a strike of ₹220 costs ₹4. It is OTM, so its intrinsic value is 0 and the whole ₹4 is time value. Aarav loves that it is cheap. Meera points out the share must rise more than ₹10 just to break even.

🧪 TRY IT: SPLIT IT
A fictional share trades at ₹300. A put with a strike of ₹320 has a premium of ₹28. What is its intrinsic value and time value, and is it ITM or OTM?
(Answer: intrinsic value = 320 - 300 = ₹20 and time value = 28 - 20 = ₹8. The put is in the money, because the strike is above the price.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Premium is intrinsic value plus time value. OTM options are cheap because they usually fail, not because they are bargains.

quiz.question: What is the premium made of?
quiz.explanation: Premium = intrinsic value + time value.

quiz.question: A share is at ₹210 and a call has a strike of ₹200. What is its intrinsic value?
When is a call out of the money?
quiz.explanation: A call is OTM when the price is below the strike.

quiz.question: The premium is ₹15 and intrinsic value is ₹10. What is the time value?
What is the time value at the exact moment of expiry?
quiz.explanation: Only intrinsic value remains at expiry.

submodules.title: 8. Time Decay and Volatility
submodules.intro: Why can an option lose value even when the share does not move?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: TIME DECAY AND VOLATILITY
Options are a wasting asset. Their time value melts away as expiry gets closer, which is called time decay. How much you pay also depends on how much the market expects the price to swing, called implied volatility. Both can make a correct view lose money. Derivatives are high-risk and only for adults, so use this lesson to learn and practise on a simulator. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
If a share does not move at all, an option's price usually still drifts down toward its intrinsic value as expiry approaches.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: TIME DECAY
• Time value shrinks every day, and the loss usually speeds up in the last days before expiry.
• Theta is the name for the daily loss of value.
• Buyers fight time decay. Sellers collect it, but they carry large risk.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: VOLATILITY
• Historical volatility: how much the price actually moved in the past.
• Implied volatility (IV): how much movement the option price is assuming for the future.
• Higher IV means higher premiums. Lower IV means lower premiums.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: EVENT RISK
• Before big events such as results or policy announcements, IV tends to rise.
• After the event, uncertainty drops, IV falls, and premiums can fall sharply even if the price moved in your favour. This is sometimes called a volatility crush.
• Many beginners buy options before an event and lose money anyway.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE SHRINKING PREMIUM
A fictional at-the-money call is bought for ₹20, which is all time value, with 30 days to expiry. The share does not move. With 10 days left, the premium is ₹8. The buyer has lost 20 - 8 = ₹12 per share, which is 12 ÷ 20 x 100 = 60% of the premium. Nothing went wrong with the share. Time just passed.

🧪 TRY IT: MEASURE THE DECAY
A fictional option has a time value of ₹50 with 20 days left. With 5 days left and the share unchanged, it is ₹10. How much time value was lost, and what percentage is that?
(Answer: 50 - 10 = ₹40 lost, which is 40 ÷ 50 x 100 = 80% of the time value.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Time decay and falling volatility can shrink an option's price even when the share goes your way. Be especially careful with options near expiry and around big events.

quiz.question: What is time decay?
options: The loss of an option's time value as expiry approaches
quiz.explanation: Time value melts away as expiry nears.

quiz.question: What does implied volatility describe?
options: How much movement the option price is assuming
quiz.explanation: IV shows the expected size of price swings.

quiz.question: What usually happens to premiums when IV rises?
quiz.explanation: Higher IV means higher option premiums.

quiz.question: An option's time value falls from ₹20 to ₹8 with no share move. What percentage of it was lost?
Why can options lose value right after a big event even if the price moved your way?
options: Volatility falls and the premium drops
quiz.explanation: Falling implied volatility can cut the premium.

submodules.title: 9. The Greeks in Plain Words
submodules.intro: What do delta, theta and vega tell you about an option?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: THE GREEKS IN PLAIN WORDS
The Greeks are measures of how an option's price reacts to different things. You do not need advanced maths to use the idea. They help you see why an option moved and what could hurt you next. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Delta is often used as a rough guide to the chance an option finishes in the money, so a delta of 0.3 is a loose way of saying about a 30% chance.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: DELTA
• Delta: roughly how much the option price changes for a ₹1 move in the underlying.
• Calls have delta between 0 and 1. Puts have delta between 0 and -1.
• An at-the-money option has a delta of about 0.5. Deep in the money options have deltas near 1, and far out of the money options near 0.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THETA, VEGA, GAMMA
• Theta: the rupees an option loses per day from time passing. It is usually negative for buyers.
• Vega: how much the price changes for a 1 point change in implied volatility.
• Gamma: how fast delta itself changes. It is highest for at-the-money options near expiry, which is why they can swing wildly.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: USING THEM
• The Greeks are estimates and change as the price, time and volatility change.
• Check the delta, theta and vega before you buy, so you know what moves you are betting on.

🍕 MINI CASE: A DELTA EXAMPLE
A fictional call has a delta of 0.5 and a premium of ₹10. The share rises by ₹4. The premium should rise by about 0.5 x 4 = ₹2, to about ₹12. For a lot of 100, that is about ₹200. Meanwhile, the option has a theta of -1.5, so each day it quietly loses about ₹1.50 per share. After 4 days, that is about 4 x 1.5 = ₹6 per share from time alone.

🧪 TRY IT: ESTIMATE THE MOVE
A fictional call has a delta of 0.3 and the share rises ₹10. A fictional put has a delta of -0.4 and the share falls ₹5. Estimate the change in each option's premium.
(Answer: the call rises by about 0.3 x 10 = ₹3. The put rises by about 0.4 x 5 = ₹2, because a falling share helps a put.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Delta shows how much an option follows the share, theta shows what time takes away, and vega shows the effect of volatility. They are guides, not guarantees.

quiz.question: What does delta show?
options: About how much the option price changes per ₹1 move in the underlying
quiz.explanation: Delta links option price changes to underlying moves.

quiz.question: An at-the-money option usually has a delta of about...
quiz.explanation: ATM options have a delta near 0.5.

quiz.question: A call with a delta of 0.5 sees the share rise ₹4. About how much does the premium rise?
What does theta measure?
options: The value lost per day as time passes
quiz.explanation: Theta is the daily time decay.

quiz.question: Which Greek measures sensitivity to implied volatility?
quiz.explanation: Vega shows the effect of volatility changes.

submodules.title: 10. Hedging and Defined-Risk Strategies
submodules.intro: How can options limit your downside instead of adding risk?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: HEDGING AND DEFINED-RISK STRATEGIES
Options can be used like insurance. A hedge costs money, the premium, and in return it limits how much you can lose. Defined-risk strategies are built so that you know the worst case before you start. Derivatives are high-risk and only for adults, so use this lesson to learn and practise on a simulator. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A protective put works like an insurance policy on a share you own. You pay a premium and, in return, your loss is capped.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: PROTECTIVE PUT
• You own a share and buy a put option on it.
• If the share falls below the strike, the put gains and offsets the loss.
• Maximum loss per share = (purchase price - strike) + premium.
• The cost is the premium, which also lowers your profit if the share rises.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: BULL CALL SPREAD
• Buy a call at a lower strike and sell a call at a higher strike.
• Net cost = premium paid - premium received.
• Maximum loss = net cost. Maximum profit = difference in strikes - net cost.
• Breakeven = lower strike + net cost.
• It costs less than a single call but caps your profit.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: IMPORTANT
• Hedging reduces risk, not eliminates it, and always has a cost.
• Selling a call or put on its own, without protection, is not a defined-risk strategy.
• Learn these on a simulator before even thinking about real money.

🍕 MINI CASE: INSURANCE ON A SHARE
In her simulator, Meera owns a fictional share bought at ₹200, lot size 100. She buys a put with a strike of ₹190 for a premium of ₹5. Her maximum loss per share is (200 - 190) + 5 = ₹15, which is ₹1,500 per lot. If the share rises to ₹230, her gain is (230 - 200) - 5 = ₹25 per share. For a spread, buying a call at ₹200 for ₹10 and selling a call at ₹210 for ₹4 costs ₹6, so the maximum loss is ₹6, the maximum profit is 10 - 6 = ₹4, and breakeven is ₹206.

🧪 TRY IT: PRICE THE PROTECTION
A fictional share is held at ₹500, lot size 50. A put with a strike of ₹480 costs ₹12. What is the maximum loss per share, and per lot?
(Answer: (500 - 480) + 12 = ₹32 per share, so 32 x 50 = ₹1,600 per lot.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Hedges and spreads put a limit on losses at a cost. Know your worst case in rupees before you enter, and avoid selling options without protection.

quiz.question: What is a protective put?
options: Buying a put on a share you own
quiz.explanation: It is insurance for a share you hold.

quiz.question: A share is bought at ₹200, a ₹190 put costs ₹5. What is the maximum loss per share?
Buy a ₹200 call for ₹10 and sell a ₹210 call for ₹4. What is the maximum loss per share?
quiz.explanation: Net cost is 10 - 4 = ₹6, which is the maximum loss.

quiz.question: What is the breakeven of that spread?
quiz.explanation: Lower strike 200 + net cost 6 = ₹206.

quiz.question: Does hedging remove all risk?
options: No, it reduces risk at a cost
quiz.explanation: A hedge costs money and still leaves some risk.

submodules.title: 11. Why Most Beginners Lose
submodules.intro: What does the evidence say about trading derivatives?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: WHY MOST BEGINNERS LOSE
Studies by SEBI, India's market regulator, have found that around nine in ten individual traders in futures and options lose money, and many lose year after year. This lesson looks at why, so you can understand the risk. Derivatives trading is only for adults, and brokers require extra checks. For you, the right place is a simulator. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
In those SEBI studies, losses were large for the average trader, and the costs of trading made the results worse.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE MAIN REASONS
• Leverage: small moves create big losses.
• Time decay: option buyers lose value daily.
• Costs: brokerage, taxes and other charges add up with every trade.
• Overtrading: many small trades, many costs.
• Expiry-day gambling: buying very cheap options on the last day, hoping for a miracle.
• Selling options for small premiums and then facing a huge loss on a sudden move.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE SELLER'S TRAP
• An option seller wins a small amount most of the time and loses a large amount rarely.
• It can feel safe until one gap move erases many months of gains.
• The maximum gain is the premium. The loss can be many times larger.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: EXPECTANCY AND COSTS
• Expectancy = win rate x average win - loss rate x average loss.
• Subtract costs from every trade. A rule with zero expectancy before costs loses money after costs.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE LOPSIDED SELLER
A fictional trader sells a call with a strike of ₹200 for a premium of ₹5, lot size 100. The most that can be gained is 5 x 100 = ₹500. The share gaps up to ₹240 on news. The loss per share is (240 - 200) - 5 = ₹35, which is ₹3,500 per lot, or 7 times the best possible gain. A different trader wins 40% of trades with an average win of ₹3,000 and an average loss of ₹2,000. Expectancy = 0.4 x 3,000 - 0.6 x 2,000 = 1,200 - 1,200 = ₹0. With costs of ₹150 per trade, the result is -₹150 per trade.

🧪 TRY IT: SIZE THE DANGER
A fictional trader sells a put with a strike of ₹300 for a premium of ₹6, lot size 50. The share falls to ₹260. What is the loss per lot, and what was the maximum possible gain?
(Answer: the loss per share is (300 - 260) - 6 = ₹34, so 34 x 50 = ₹1,700 per lot. The maximum gain was 6 x 50 = ₹300.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Most individual derivatives traders lose money because of leverage, decay, costs and overtrading. Treat this area with great respect and practise only on a simulator until you are an adult.

quiz.question: What have SEBI studies found about individual futures and options traders?
options: Around nine in ten lose money
quiz.explanation: The SEBI studies found that a large majority lose money.

quiz.question: Which of these is a common reason beginners lose?
quiz.explanation: Costs, leverage and overtrading hurt most beginners.

quiz.question: An option seller receives ₹5 per share and the share gap makes the loss ₹35 per share. The loss is how many times the premium?
quiz.explanation: 35 ÷ 5 = 7 times.

quiz.question: A rule has an expectancy of ₹0 before costs and costs are ₹150 per trade. What is the result per trade?
Who may trade derivatives, and where should kids practise?
options: Adults only, and kids should practise on a simulator
quiz.explanation: Derivatives are for adults, and a simulator is the safe way to learn.

submodules.title: 12. Your Derivatives Checklist and Journal
submodules.intro: How do you put every lesson into one careful routine?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: THE DERIVATIVES CHECKLIST
You have studied futures, margin, pricing, options, payoffs, time decay, the Greeks, hedging and the risks. This capstone turns it into a checklist and a journal for your simulator practice. The goal is a careful, repeatable routine, not fast profit. Derivatives are high-risk and only for adults, so use this lesson to learn and practise on a simulator. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Many professional traders keep a journal, because it shows their own repeated habits, both good and bad.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE CHECKLIST
1. Purpose: am I hedging a risk or just practising a view?
2. View: what does the trend and the market say?
3. Contract: type (call, put or future), strike and expiry.
4. Maximum loss: the rupee amount I can lose, known before I enter.
5. Size: the maximum loss is no more than about 1% of my simulator capital.
6. Time and events: how many days are left, how much theta, and is there an event ahead?
7. Costs: what will charges take from the trade?
8. Exit plan: target, stop-loss and a time limit written down.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE JOURNAL
After every trade, write the date, the contract, your reason, entry, exit, result, how you felt and what you would change. Review the journal each month. It turns vague regret into a specific fix.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: COMMON TRAPS
• Buying cheap options in the last days before expiry.
• Trading to win back a loss.
• Selling options without protection.
• Using the full margin available.
• Changing the plan in the middle of a trade.

🍕 MINI CASE: LEARNING FROM THE JOURNAL
Meera has ₹1,00,000 in her simulator, so 1% is ₹1,000. A call with a premium of ₹8 and a lot size of 100 costs ₹800 at most, so one lot fits her limit. After 15 practice trades she wins 6, a win rate of 6 ÷ 15 x 100 = 40%. Her journal shows that 7 of her 9 losses came from options bought with fewer than 5 days to expiry. She adds a rule: only buy options with at least 15 days left.

🧪 TRY IT: BUILD YOUR OWN
Fill in the eight checklist lines for an imaginary trade. Then work out how many lots you can take: with ₹2,00,000 in the simulator, risk of 1%, and a premium of ₹10 with a lot size of 50, how many lots fit?
(Answer: 1% of ₹2,00,000 is ₹2,000. One lot costs 10 x 50 = ₹500, so 2,000 ÷ 500 = 4 lots. Discuss your notes with a parent, teacher or guardian.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
A checklist keeps you careful and a journal keeps you honest. No method guarantees profit, so practise on a simulator and involve a parent or guardian in any real money decision.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the derivatives checklist?
options: To bring the main checks and a risk limit into one routine
quiz.explanation: The checklist keeps your analysis and risk consistent.

quiz.question: Simulator capital is ₹1,00,000 and you risk 1%. What is the maximum loss per trade?
Out of 15 trades, 6 are wins. What is the win rate?
Why keep a trading journal?
options: It shows your repeated habits and helps fix mistakes
quiz.explanation: A journal turns vague regret into specific fixes.

quiz.question: Does any checklist guarantee profit in derivatives?
options: No, risk always remains, so practise on a simulator and involve a parent or guardian
quiz.explanation: No method removes risk.
